analysis.one_liner: Mandates mold cleanup, inspections, and oversight for military housing run by private landlords.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in June 2020 to fix mold and oversight problems in military housing, never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Military families living in government-backed, privately managed housing had reported serious mold and maintenance problems. This bill would require mold cleanup guidance, reimbursement for damaged belongings, public disclosure of how the Department of Defense rates the private landlords, emergency relocation rules when mold makes a home unlivable, and extension of housing standards to government-owned military homes. It also would place liaisons to help families with special-needs members and require a report on Pentagon follow-through on a March 2020 watchdog report. It was referred to the Armed Services Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Military families living in privatized and government-owned military housing, especially those dealing with mold, displaced during repairs, or with special-needs family members.

how_it_helps.text: Requires mold mitigation measures, reimbursement for personal property lost to mold damage or cleanup, and procedures for returning families displaced during mitigation [S2] [S3].

Establishes a working group, including the Armed Forces' Surgeons General, to set best practices for mold mitigation and to define when mold is an emergency requiring relocation of residents [S2] [S3].

Requires public disclosure of the criteria and metrics DOD uses to rate the performance of private landlords that receive incentive fees, allowing families and Congress to see how those companies are judged [S2] [S3].

Expands the uniform code of basic housing standards and inspection requirements to cover government-owned and government-controlled military family housing inside and outside the United States [S2] [S3].
Requires each military department to appoint at least one Exceptional Family Member Program housing liaison to help families with special needs obtain services [S2] [S3].
Requires a report within 180 days on Pentagon progress implementing a March 2020 GAO report's recommendations on oversight of privatized housing [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The private landlords who manage privatized military housing, who would face mold mitigation costs, property reimbursement obligations, and public performance metrics, plus administrative costs for the Defense Department.

drawbacks.text: Much of the bill directs guidance and reports rather than immediate fixes; families already living with mold would have to wait for working groups, standards, and Pentagon paperwork to translate into actual repairs.

Mold remediation, relocation, and reimbursement requirements would add costs for the private landlords, who could argue for recovering them through the housing allowance payments military families already direct to them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For affected military families, the health and habitability gains outweigh the administrative costs, though the bill leans on guidance and reports rather than deadlines for physical repairs, so its real-world impact would depend on DOD follow-through.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never acted and no vote ever happened before that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Kendra Horn introduced the bill on June 15, 2020, joined by three Republican and one Democratic cosponsor [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Armed Services Committee the same day and received no further action through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private landlords that manage privatized military housing avoided new mold remediation, reimbursement, and public performance-reporting requirements, and the Pentagon avoided additional oversight reporting.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but modest; the bill drew no recorded opposition because it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Private landlords managing privatized military housing
industries.note: The bill would require them to handle mold mitigation, reimburse damaged belongings, and have their performance judged by publicly disclosed metrics, all costs and scrutiny that military families currently bear through substandard housing.
